content.headline: Ukraine peace talks resume as both sides show limited private flexibility, US官
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine talks resume amid limited signs of flexibility
content.standfirst: Delegations from Ukraine, Russia and the US are due to meet in Abu Dhabi for the first trilateral talks since February. The sides remain far apart on territory and postwar security, and a breakthrough is not expected.

image.caption: The talks come after a deadly Russian strike on a village in Zaporizhzhia, according to the BBC.

sources.originalTitle: Ukraine peace talks resume with 'some flexibility' by warring sides, US officials say

segments.body: Officials from Moscow, Kyiv and Washington are due to meet in Abu Dhabi. A US official says both Russia and Ukraine have shown “a little bit of flexibility” privately over the future of eastern Ukraine, but neither side has shifted its public position on the contested Donetsk region.

segments.title: Territory and security
segments.body: Russia wants Ukraine to give up the parts of Donetsk it still controls; Kyiv says the front line should be frozen. The US official said any agreement on territory depends on a postwar security arrangement. Proposals include security consultations, crisis hotlines and reciprocal de-escalation measures.

European leaders, largely excluded from previous discussions, want a role in decisions affecting their continent’s security. The US says it will propose a wider format involving Europeans, but it is unclear whether Moscow would agree. Ukraine continues to face Russian strikes on its territory and energy infrastructure.

perspectives.body: Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko told the BBC he fears President Trump wants a quick deal at Ukraine’s expense. He argued that sanctions and military pressure, rather than concessions, are needed to persuade Vladimir Putin to negotiate.

content.headline: Trump says FBI is investigating Nvidia chief’s relationship with alleged Chinese
content.shortHeadline: Trump says FBI is investigating Nvidia chief’s relationship
content.standfirst: Donald Trump says he spoke to Jensen Huang and believes the Nvidia chief did not know his former business associate was allegedly a Chinese spy. The FBI has declined to comment, and the company says it has no evidence secrets were compromised.

image.caption: Donald Trump stands with Nvidia chief Jensen Huang in Washington.

sources.originalTitle: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
Silicon Valley and Trump rally behind Nvidia CEO after his affair with alleged Chinese spy
The AI poster boy, the ‘Chinese spy’ and Trump: how an affair may have harmed US security

segments.body: Trump said the FBI was looking into Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based businesswoman whom US officials reportedly suspect of spying for China. The president said he asked the Nvidia chief whether he knew she was a spy; Huang reportedly denied it. The FBI declined to comment, and the timing and scope of any inquiry have not been made public.

segments.title: Security questions remain
segments.body: Nvidia’s board has begun an independent investigation. The company says it has no reason to believe its trade secrets or US national security were compromised. China has rejected the allegations as groundless. Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are not related, and she has not publicly responded to the claims.

The scrutiny reaches beyond the relationship: Nvidia’s chips are central to the US-China competition over artificial intelligence, and Jensen Huang has lobbied for looser export controls on sales to China. The company’s shares fell more than 4% on Monday, according to the BBC.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s analysis points to Huang’s access to Trump and his role in US chip-export policy as reasons the allegations have drawn national-security attention. It notes that the inquiry has not established that sensitive information was passed to China.

content.headline: Climate report finds fossil-fuel emissions near a plateau, but total emissions
content.shortHeadline: Fossil-fuel emissions near a plateau, climate report says
content.standfirst: A new assessment says emissions from oil, gas and coal are forecast to edge down only slightly in 2026, while deforestation pushes total emissions higher. Separately, the UN weather agency reports accelerating heat accumulation and record ocean warmth.

image.caption: Flooding in Chattogram, Bangladesh, in April illustrated the impacts of climate-related weather extremes.

sources.originalTitle: Slight fall in carbon emissions from fossil fuels as Iran war drives renewables push
‘A new age of climate extremes’: Earth accumulating heat at accelerating rate
High fossil fuel prices spread inflation ‘like a cancer’, UN climate chief tells Cop31

segments.body: The Global Carbon Budget assessment forecasts a 0.4% fall in emissions from fossil fuels in 2026, a change its authors caution may be temporary. Increased emissions from deforestation and land-use change mean total carbon emissions are forecast to rise slightly, to 43.3bn tonnes.

segments.title: Heat continues to build
segments.body: The World Meteorological Organization says the imbalance between energy entering and leaving Earth reached its highest level since monitoring began. January to September temperatures averaged about 1.47C above the pre-industrial level, while ocean heat and sea levels reached records, according to the agency.

segments.title: Talks under pressure
segments.body: The findings arrive as COP31 opens in Antalya, where Turkey and Australia are promoting a voluntary goal to increase electricity’s share of final energy use to one-third by 2035. Scientists say the world’s remaining carbon budget for limiting warming to 1.5C is less than four years at current emissions rates.

perspectives.body: The assessment’s authors warn that a one-year dip is not proof that emissions have peaked. The fall in fossil-fuel emissions is small, may reverse, and is more than offset by emissions from land-use change.

content.headline: Trump says further US attacks on Iran are ‘highly unlikely’ as talks continue
content.shortHeadline: Trump says further US attacks on Iran are unlikely
content.standfirst: The president says Washington is maintaining its blockade while pursuing negotiations, but that US forces remain ready to act. Iranian officials have previously expressed doubt about his claims of progress towards ending the conflict.

image.caption: Donald Trump speaks to reporters about the conflict with Iran.

sources.originalTitle: Trump says more US attacks on Iran 'highly unlikely'
Trump says US war in Iran ‘effectively over’ as he plays down escalation concerns

segments.body: Donald Trump said renewed US attacks on Iran were “highly unlikely” and that the situation would remain at the “status quo” for now. He also said US forces were “locked and loaded” should circumstances change, without declaring an end to the conflict.

The comments followed a meeting with Qatar’s prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani, who said he had discussed reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region. Trump described the talks as positive, but Iranian officials have previously questioned his assertions about resolving the conflict.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that Trump has repeatedly overstated the status of negotiations during the nearly nine-month war. Gulf states, including Qatar, have urged him not to resume fighting.

content.headline: France accuses Iran’s Revolutionary Guard of supermarket fridge cyberattack
content.shortHeadline: France blames Iran’s Revolutionary Guard for fridge cyberattack
content.standfirst: France says Iran’s Revolutionary Guard was behind an attack that raised temperatures in supermarket refrigerators, spoiling food. Tehran has not officially responded, and French authorities have not explained how they attributed the attack.

image.caption: Supermarket refrigerators and freezers in France were affected by the reported cyberattack.

sources.originalTitle: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking

segments.body: French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot accused Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of a cyberattack that affected supermarket refrigeration in October. He called it unprecedented in scale and said France had summoned Iran’s ambassador. Iran has not officially responded; some Iranian media have dismissed the accusation.

segments.title: Attribution remains uncertain
segments.body: The attack affected hundreds of stores, with temperatures in some fridges reportedly reaching 50C. The systems were supplied by Danish engineering firm Danfoss. A second wave of attacks affected stores in several European countries, but it is not known whether the incidents are linked. France has not detailed the evidence behind its accusation.

perspectives.body: The BBC notes that cyberattacks are difficult to attribute because attackers can conceal their location. Earlier claims by Russian-aligned groups to be responsible were not widely believed.

content.headline: Turkey steelworks blast kills at least 17 workers during maintenance
content.shortHeadline: At least 17 killed in Turkey steelworks blast
content.standfirst: A blast and fire at the Habas Demir Celik plant near Izmir killed at least 17 workers and injured 12, authorities say. Investigators are examining the collapse of a crane carrying a replacement boiler during maintenance.

image.caption: Smoke rose from the Habas Demir Celik factory after the explosion.

sources.originalTitle: Turkey steel factory blast kills at least 17 people

segments.body: At least 17 workers were killed and 12 injured in an explosion at the Habas Demir Celik steelworks in Aliaga, near Izmir. The local governor said a crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed, sending material into a furnace. The company said the accident happened during scheduled maintenance.

Search and rescue operations continued after the blast, and some people were believed to be under rubble, the governor said. At least five people had been arrested, according to reports cited by the BBC’s Turkish service. The cause of the collapse has not been established.

content.headline: Trump administration loses more than 10,000 federal lawyers as senior staff
content.shortHeadline: US justice department faces lawyer exodus and senior resignations
content.standfirst: Four senior Justice Department lawyers have resigned in less than a week, while more than 10,000 federal lawyers are reported to have left since Donald Trump took office. Former officials and judges warn the departures are straining the work of the courts.

image.caption: US Attorney General Todd Blanche announced the departure of several key attorneys after the midterms.

sources.originalTitle: Trump has a growing problem – his lawyers are leaving

segments.body: Four high-profile Justice Department lawyers have resigned in less than a week, including officials from its civil rights and national security divisions, according to the i Paper. The article cites estimates that more than 10,000 federal lawyers have left since the start of the Trump administration, with departures outpacing hiring.

segments.title: Strain in the courts
segments.body: The report describes heavier caseloads for remaining lawyers and concerns from judges about missed court orders and the reliability of government submissions. The reasons for the recent senior departures have not been confirmed publicly; speculation has linked them to the administration’s handling of investigations and prosecutions.

content.headline: Qantas to move most of 850 corporate jobs to India under Accenture deal
content.shortHeadline: Qantas to outsource 850 jobs, mostly to India
content.standfirst: The Australian airline says the changes, expected to begin in mid-2027, will modernise its technology systems. Staff will be redeployed where possible, while unions and employees are being consulted.

image.caption: Qantas chief executive Vanessa Hudson apologised for the uncertainty caused by the job cuts.

sources.originalTitle: Qantas to outsource 850 local jobs with most roles moving to India

segments.body: Qantas plans to outsource 850 corporate jobs to Accenture, with most of the work moving to India and some remaining in Australia. The airline says the changes will begin in mid-2027 and affect areas including finance, procurement, people and marketing.

Chief executive Vanessa Hudson said the deal is intended to modernise systems built up over decades and reduce duplication. Qantas says it will redeploy affected staff where possible, including into new roles in Australia; discussions with unions and employees are under way.

content.headline: Jemima Goldsmith says Russell Brand subjected her to violence and abuse
content.shortHeadline: Jemima Goldsmith accuses Russell Brand of violence and abuse
content.standfirst: Goldsmith says she called police during a violent incident at her home in 2014 but did not press charges, citing concern for her children. The claims are separate from Brand’s convictions for rape and sexual assault.

image.caption: Jemima Goldsmith and Russell Brand dated for about a year in the mid-2010s.

sources.originalTitle: Russell Brand's ex Jemima Goldsmith accuses him of violence and abuse against her
Jemima Goldsmith says ex-partner Russell Brand physically assaulted her

segments.body: Jemima Goldsmith says her former partner Russell Brand subjected her to “violence, coercive control and abuse” during their relationship. She says she called police to have him removed from her home in 2014 but did not pursue charges because she worried about the effect of publicity on her teenage children.

segments.title: Separate from the convictions
segments.body: Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison after being convicted of rape and sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents between 2004 and 2009. Goldsmith says she has not seen or spoken to him since 2014. Her allegations about their relationship have not been tested in court.

perspectives.body: Goldsmith also addressed a separate 2014 harassment injunction involving a woman who had alleged an assault by Brand. She says she did not witness anything untoward during that woman’s visit and that police found no case to answer.

content.headline: Palantir urged minister to bring NHS GP records into its data platform
content.shortHeadline: Palantir lobbied to add GP records to its NHS data platform
content.standfirst: Messages obtained under freedom of information rules show Palantir pressing a health minister to consider linking GP records to its NHS platform, despite an earlier pledge that such data would be excluded. Doctors warn that the move could undermine patient trust.

image.caption: GP records were excluded from Palantir’s existing NHS data platform contract.

sources.originalTitle: Revealed: Palantir lobbied minister to stretch AI tools’ reach to NHS GP records

segments.body: WhatsApp messages between Palantir’s UK chief, Louis Mosley, and former health minister Zubir Ahmed show the company arguing that linking GP and hospital data would benefit the NHS. The exchanges, obtained by campaign group Foxglove, took place from July 2025 to March 2026, according to the Guardian.

segments.title: Trust and scope
segments.body: GP data was expressly excluded from Palantir’s £330m contract to run NHS England’s federated data platform. The British Medical Association and patient advocates have opposed bringing it into the system, warning that patients may lose trust if they do not know who can access their records.

perspectives.body: Palantir says data sharing can improve the NHS and that its software preserves local control of data. It says decisions about how the platform is used belong to the government.

segments.body: The government has not announced a decision to add GP records. The health secretary says a review of the contract is continuing, while ministers have spoken of developing UK “sovereign AI” for the health service.

content.headline: More than half of surveyed English headteachers consider leaving early after Of
content.shortHeadline: Ofsted inspections prompt many surveyed heads to consider leaving
content.standfirst: A survey of 242 school leaders found 52% were considering leaving their role sooner than planned after inspections under Ofsted’s new system. The watchdog says it is working with ministers to reduce pressure while maintaining accountability.

image.caption: Many school leaders say the new Ofsted inspection system has increased pressure.

sources.originalTitle: Headteachers consider leaving jobs earlier than planned after new Ofsted inspection

segments.body: In a survey by the National Association of Head Teachers, 52% of respondents said an Ofsted inspection had made them consider leaving their job earlier than planned. Nearly two-thirds said the new inspections were much more intense than the previous framework, and 86% reported difficulty with their wellbeing while inspectors were on site.

segments.title: Ofsted response
segments.body: The inspection changes were introduced a year ago after criticism of the strain caused by the previous system. Ofsted says many school leaders have found inspections helpful, while acknowledging others raised concerns about workload and wellbeing. The Department for Education says inspections should be fair and focused on helping schools improve.

perspectives.body: The survey was conducted by the headteachers’ union and had 242 responses between June and October. Ofsted says it is working with the education secretary on ways to reduce pressure without losing focus on children and families.

content.headline: Prince William calls for better protection from sexual harassment in armed
content.shortHeadline: Prince William calls for stronger protection for service women
content.standfirst: The Prince of Wales says the military is not consistently meeting standards of respect and safety for women. A Ministry of Defence survey cited in his article found 67% of service women had faced unwanted sexualised behaviour each year.

image.caption: Prince William held fact-finding meetings with women serving in the armed forces.

sources.originalTitle: Prince William wants more protection from harassment for service women

segments.body: Prince William says more must be done to protect women in the armed forces from sexual harassment. After private meetings with service women across the Army, Royal Navy and Royal Air Force, he wrote that some did not feel safe, respected or valued.

His article cites a Ministry of Defence survey in which 67% of service women said they had faced unwanted sexualised behaviour each year, while 30% had considered leaving. Women told him about inappropriate comments, rumours and harassment in barracks. The chief of the defence staff acknowledged that their experiences had not always met expected standards.

content.headline: UK rail cyberattack could cause week of disruption and cost £1.8bn, report
content.shortHeadline: Hypothetical rail cyberattack could cost £1.8bn, report says
content.standfirst: A government-commissioned scenario estimates that a week-long attack on rail communications could cause widespread disruption and £1.8bn in economic losses. The Department for Transport assessed the likelihood of such a major incident as low.

image.caption: The government wants to strengthen the rail network’s resilience to cyber threats.

sources.originalTitle: How Putin could bring Britain’s railways to a halt

segments.body: A Department for Transport resilience report describes a hypothetical cyberattack on rail communications that could disrupt services for a week and cost the economy £1.8bn, including passenger delays. The research assessed the likelihood of that scenario as low.

segments.title: Preparing for disruption
segments.body: The report calls for better information-sharing, stress tests and mapping of critical infrastructure over the next five to 10 years. Experts say disruption to communications could force trains to stop or run at reduced speeds, but no attack on train operations is reported in this article.

perspectives.body: The Department for Transport describes the scenario as severe but unlikely, and says the research is intended to help operators plan and strengthen resilience.

content.headline: M&S, Amazon and other employers pledge opportunities for people out of work
content.shortHeadline: Major employers pledge jobs and training opportunities for people out
content.standfirst: Retailers and other companies say they will offer opportunities to young people and adults returning after illness or time away from work. The pledge comes ahead of a government review of youth unemployment expected later this month.

image.caption: M&S is among employers that have pledged to create opportunities for people out of work.

sources.originalTitle: From M&S to Amazon, the jobs people could be offered to keep them off benefits

segments.body: Major employers including M&S, Amazon, Pret and NatWest have signed a pledge to offer opportunities to people out of work, including young people and adults returning after illness. The Jobs Foundation says participating firms will support people to enter work and progress.

segments.title: Policy proposals ahead
segments.body: The pledge comes as the government prepares to publish Alan Milburn’s review of youth unemployment. The TUC is separately calling for an expanded Jobs Guarantee, which would fund six-month paid jobs for more young people. The employers’ pledge does not specify how many jobs will be created.

perspectives.body: The TUC says widening eligibility for its Jobs Guarantee would have upfront costs but could deliver longer-term savings. The government says it has pledged £2.5bn for youth employment support.

content.headline: Nordea fined 155m kroner after court acquits bank on most money-laundering
content.shortHeadline: Nordea fine is far below prosecutors’ demand after most counts fail
content.standfirst: A Copenhagen court fined Nordea 155m kroner, far below the 6.6bn kroner sought by prosecutors, and acquitted it on five of seven counts. A new assessment from a money-laundering expert calls the result a setback for the prosecution.

image.caption: Nordea’s Vesterport branch was at the centre of the case over customer transactions.

sources.originalTitle: Ekspert revser anklagemyndighed efter Nordea-dom: Pinligt og noget af en mavepuster

segments.body: Nordea was fined 155m kroner for money-laundering law violations after a case that began more than a decade ago. The court acquitted the bank on five of seven counts, including the main allegation concerning transactions by 25 eastern European customers through its Copenhagen branch between 2012 and 2015.

segments.title: A setback for prosecutors
segments.body: Prosecutors had sought a 6.6bn-kroner fine, arguing that the bank had failed to investigate transactions worth nearly 25bn kroner. A CBS lecturer specialising in anti-money-laundering rules described the outcome as a major setback. Prosecutors say they will review the judgment before deciding whether to appeal.

perspectives.body: The prosecution says the court found Nordea had committed several violations, but accepts that it was acquitted on substantial parts of the case. The bank says it is satisfied with the outcome.

content.headline: Greenland’s Atassut leaves coalition, but government retains a majority
content.shortHeadline: Atassut quits Greenland coalition; government keeps its majority
content.standfirst: Atassut says a minister should resign over a grant to an association, a demand she has rejected. The party’s departure leaves the governing coalition with 18 of Greenland’s 31 parliamentary seats.

sources.originalTitle: Partiet Atassut træder ud af Grønlands regeringskoalition

segments.body: The Greenlandic party Atassut has decided to leave the governing coalition, public broadcaster KNR reported, citing a decision by the party’s executive board. Atassut says Nivi Olsen, the minister for education, culture, sport and church, should resign over a grant to an association. Olsen has rejected the demand.
The coalition will now comprise Demokraatit and Inuit Ataqatigiit. Together they hold 18 of the 31 seats in Greenland’s parliament and retain a majority.

content.headline: Danish climate minister criticised for taking private jet to COP31
content.shortHeadline: Climate minister faces criticism over private flight to COP31
content.standfirst: Samira Nawa travelled to Antalya on a chartered plane while accompanying Queen Mary. Climate advocates and an opposition politician say the choice sends the wrong signal; the minister says it made sense to travel on the same flight as the Queen.

image.caption: Queen Mary and climate minister Samira Nawa travelled together to the climate summit on a private charter.

sources.originalTitle: Klimaminister flyver med dronning Mary i privatfly til klimatopmøde

segments.body: Climate minister Samira Nawa flew to COP31 in Antalya on a chartered aircraft while accompanying Queen Mary, the ministry confirmed to DR. Oxfam Denmark and the Alternative party criticised the decision, arguing that private flights are particularly carbon-intensive and undermine the government’s climate message.

segments.title: Minister’s explanation
segments.body: Nawa said she travelled on a full flight with the Queen and that accompanying her made it logical to use the same plane. The royal household said the trip followed the usual guidelines for official travel. The reporting does not specify the emissions from this particular flight.

content.headline: Rødding hit by more vandalism as eight municipal cars are painted
content.shortHeadline: Eight municipal cars vandalised in Rødding amid racist graffiti
content.standfirst: Police say the latest damage may be linked to a series of incidents involving racist messages in the southern Jutland town. Officers walked through Rødding with residents to hear ideas for improving safety.

image.caption: Municipal cars in Rødding were vandalised overnight.

sources.originalTitle: Nyt hærværk i Rødding: Kommunens biler overmalet med racistiske ord

segments.body: Eight municipal vehicles in Rødding were painted overnight on Monday. Police said the incident may be linked to earlier vandalism, including racist messages on buildings and cars. A week earlier, a firework damaged a pizzeria’s windows and door, and racist phrases were written on windows.

Police invited residents on a walk through the town to discuss ways to prevent further damage and improve safety. Resident Marius Kjeld Finderup said the vandalism should not be allowed to make people from other countries feel unwelcome. No arrests are reported in the supplied coverage.

content.headline: New specialist counselling planned for LGBT+ survivors of sexual abuse
content.shortHeadline: LGBT+ survivors to get specialist sexual-abuse counselling
content.standfirst: Aids-Fondet plans to launch counselling in 2027 after clinic visitors reported sexual harassment and abuse. The service will be available in person in Copenhagen and online elsewhere in Denmark.

image.caption: The new counselling service is intended for LGBT+ people who have experienced sexual abuse.

sources.originalTitle: Ny rådgivning skal hjælpe LGBT+-personer efter overgreb

segments.body: Aids-Fondet will receive 900,000 kroner a year from 2027 to 2030 to pilot specialist counselling for LGBT+ people who have experienced sexual harassment or abuse. The service will be available in person in Copenhagen and online across the rest of Denmark.

The organisation says around a third of people completing its clinic self-assessment report having experienced sexual harassment or abuse. It says existing services are used relatively little by sexual minorities, and the new advice service will also connect people with established support options.

content.headline: Danish consumer test finds large gaps between electric cars’ claimed and
content.shortHeadline: Test finds some electric cars fall far short of claimed range
content.standfirst: A Forbrugerrådet Tænk test of 44 electric cars found differences of more than 100 kilometres between advertised and measured range. The organisation says its road test includes more motorway driving than the standard used by manufacturers.

image.caption: The consumer test compared the advertised and measured range of 44 electric cars.

sources.originalTitle: Elbiler kører kortere end oplyst: Se de tre bedste og dårligste her

segments.body: A test by consumer organisation Forbrugerrådet Tænk found that some electric cars travelled more than 100 kilometres less than their advertised range. The largest percentage difference was 32.6% for a Renault Twingo, while the best-performing cars were about 6–7% below their stated range.

segments.title: Conditions matter
segments.body: Tænk says its method includes more motorway driving and changes in speed than the WLTP standard used for manufacturers’ figures. The organisation’s test lead says smaller city cars may show a larger gap when pushed to motorway speeds. Range also depends on driving conditions, and cold weather can reduce it.

perspectives.body: The Danish motorists’ organisation FDM notes that electric-car range is more sensitive to low temperatures because the battery must also power cabin heating. It says official figures remain useful as a guide, not a guarantee.

content.headline: Danish company turns coastal eelgrass into acoustic panels and expands
content.shortHeadline: Eelgrass acoustic-panel maker moves production to Sakskøbing
content.standfirst: Søuld is moving production to a former sugar factory in Lolland as it expands its acoustic products made from eelgrass gathered on Danish coasts. The company says the material absorbs sound and its products are exported abroad.

sources.originalTitle: Det stinker på stranden – men her er ålegræsset guld værd

segments.body: Danish company Søuld makes acoustic panels from eelgrass collected along the country’s coasts. It is moving production from northern Jutland to a former sugar factory in Sakskøbing, where it currently has four jobs and expects to expand.

Co-founder Kirsten Lynge says air pockets in the eelgrass fibres help absorb sound. The company exports products to the US, Australia and several European countries, and received a Danish Design Award for a product the jury praised for its sustainability. The source does not provide independent figures for the product’s environmental impact.

content.headline: Manchester United expected to sack Michael Carrick, but no decision is final
content.shortHeadline: Man Utd expected to sack Carrick, but decision not final
content.standfirst: United’s board is still expected to assess the team during the international break, but BBC Sport reports a growing expectation that senior executives will recommend Carrick’s dismissal after a poor start to the season.

image.caption: Michael Carrick signed a two-year deal with Manchester United last summer.

sources.originalTitle: Man Utd expected to sack head coach Carrick

segments.body: Manchester United are increasingly likely to sack head coach Michael Carrick, but the club has not made a final decision. BBC Sport reports that the board remains committed to reassessing his position during the international break, as planned after October’s 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth.

segments.title: A difficult start
segments.body: A growing expectation is that chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox will recommend Carrick be dismissed to minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazer family. United are 18th after 10 league matches and have won once in that run; their 4-4 draw with Aston Villa was the latest result in a season that has included three wins in 15 matches in all competitions.

content.headline: England players aired frank views on their World Cup semi-final defeat
content.shortHeadline: England players aired frank views on World Cup defeat
content.standfirst: A squad meeting with Thomas Tuchel addressed the loss to Argentina and the team’s approach late in the match. BBC Sport says players believe the discussion has helped them move on.

image.caption: Harry Kane and Jude Bellingham were among the England players who aired their views.

sources.originalTitle: Kane and Bellingham air strong views in England World Cup review

segments.body: England players are understood to have shared strong views at a “full and frank” meeting with head coach Thomas Tuchel at the start of the September international break. The discussion was part of the Football Association’s review process after England’s World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina.

segments.title: Disagreement over the closing stages
segments.body: Some players were unhappy with what they saw as an overly defensive approach after Anthony Gordon put England ahead. Argentina scored twice late on to win 2-1. Tuchel pointed to the opposition’s quality, but BBC Sport reports that players did not all accept that explanation; Harry Kane and Jude Bellingham were among those who expressed their views.

The squad is understood to feel it can move on after having its say. England lost to Spain in their first Nations League match in September, then won their next three. They are due to host Croatia on Thursday before travelling to face Spain on Sunday.

content.headline: David Warner backs Khawaja’s account of Australia’s 2018 ball-tampering
content.shortHeadline: Warner backs Khawaja over 2018 ball-tampering claims
content.standfirst: Warner says Khawaja’s account that the whole Australia team knew about the use of sandpaper is accurate, and criticises the original investigation. Cricket Australia says it remains comfortable with its findings.

image.caption: David Warner was Australia’s Test vice-captain during the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.

sources.originalTitle: Khawaja 100% accurate on ball-tampering - Warner

segments.body: Former Australia vice-captain David Warner has given his “full support” to Usman Khawaja’s claim that the entire team knew about the use of sandpaper to alter the ball during the 2018 South Africa series. Warner called Khawaja’s account “100% accurate”.

segments.title: Questions over the investigation
segments.body: Warner described Cricket Australia’s investigation as “rushed and botched”, saying Khawaja was not interviewed. Khawaja has said he was shocked not to be asked for evidence. The four bowlers named in the report have previously said they did not know a foreign substance had been taken on to the field.

Cricket Australia has not said it will reopen the inquiry. It says relevant information presented to date has been properly considered and that it remains comfortable with the findings of its integrity process. The competing accounts leave the circumstances and extent of players’ knowledge contested.

content.headline: Sabalenka fights back twice to win her WTA Finals opener
content.shortHeadline: Sabalenka battles past Muchova in WTA Finals opener
content.standfirst: The world number two recovered from a break down in both sets to beat Karolina Muchova 7-6 7-5, despite an unreliable serve. Mirra Andreeva also began with a straight-sets win.

image.caption: Aryna Sabalenka, who began her WTA Finals campaign with a win.

sources.originalTitle: Sabalenka wins WTA Finals opener despite wayward serve

segments.body: Aryna Sabalenka started her WTA Finals campaign with a 7-6 (7-2) 7-5 win over Karolina Muchova. She came back from a break down in both sets, but struggled with her serve, making seven double faults and landing 59% of her first serves.

segments.title: Andreeva also wins
segments.body: Mirra Andreeva later beat Elina Svitolina 6-4 6-0, saving all six break points she faced. Sabalenka, who has not won a Grand Slam singles title this year and is seeking her first WTA Finals crown, is playing after world number one Elena Rybakina withdrew with illness.

content.headline: Feyi-Waboso ruled out of the rest of England’s Nations Championship
content.shortHeadline: Feyi-Waboso out of Nations Championship with ankle injury
content.standfirst: The England wing injured his ankle in Sunday’s win over Australia and will miss the rest of the tournament. Several other players are also unavailable for Saturday’s match against Japan.

sources.originalTitle: England wing Feyi-Waboso out of Nations Championship

segments.body: Immanuel Feyi-Waboso will miss the rest of the Nations Championship after injuring his ankle in England’s 45-22 win over Australia. The 23-year-old was hurt in a first-half tackle by Angus Bell, for which the Australia prop received a yellow card.

segments.title: More changes for Japan
segments.body: England will also be without Seb Atkinson, Ollie Chessum and George Furbank against Japan on Saturday. Tom Curry will not play this autumn after reporting hip discomfort. England hope Atkinson, Chessum and Furbank could be available for the match against New Zealand on 21 November, but their return is not confirmed.

content.headline: Carse returns to England’s wider Test set-up as Bashir misses South Africa squad
content.shortHeadline: Carse returns to England set-up; Bashir left out of Test squad
content.standfirst: Brydon Carse is named in the Lions group as a possible cover option for England’s South Africa tour, while spinner Shoaib Bashir is omitted from the Test squad. Carse’s Cricket Regulator case remains unresolved.

image.caption: Brydon Carse has not played for England since the fifth Ashes Test in January.

sources.originalTitle: England clear way for Carse return and drop Bashir

segments.body: Brydon Carse has been named in England’s Lions squads, opening a possible route back into the Test side for the tour of South Africa. He could provide cover for Josh Tongue, who will miss the first Test for the birth of his second child. The three-Test series begins on 17 December.

segments.title: Bashir omitted
segments.body: Shoaib Bashir is left out of the Test squad, with Liam Patterson-White selected as the specialist spinner. England selector Marcus North said the decision was made for the balance of this tour and that England remained invested in Bashir. Carse, who has continued to play for Durham, has been charged by the Cricket Regulator; a verdict is still to come.

content.headline: Rob Hawkins targets another Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup final
content.shortHeadline: Hawkins targets another final after chronic fatigue battle
content.standfirst: England’s two-time World Cup winner has overcome chronic fatigue syndrome to become one of the tournament’s leading players. He is set to face Australia in Tuesday’s semi-final.

image.caption: Rob Hawkins has scored 14 tries for England at the Rugby League World Cup.

sources.originalTitle: How Hawkins overcame illness to star for England

segments.body: Rob Hawkins, who has scored 14 tries at this Rugby League World Cup, is preparing for England’s semi-final against Australia in Wollongong on Tuesday. England are aiming to take another step towards a third title and go into the match after topping Pool A.

segments.title: A route into the sport
segments.body: Hawkins took up wheelchair rugby league in 2014 after chronic fatigue syndrome had left him bedbound for 18 months. He had initially been looking for wheelchair basketball. The England and Halifax Panthers wing says he still needs extra rest at times and has learned to pace himself.

content.headline: Raul takes his first senior club management job at Real Oviedo
content.shortHeadline: Raul appointed Real Oviedo manager until 2028
content.standfirst: The former Real Madrid striker has been appointed manager of the Spanish second-division side, his first senior club job. He replaces Julian Calero, who was sacked with Oviedo ninth.

image.caption: Raul won the Champions League three times with Real Madrid.

sources.originalTitle: Real Madrid legend Raul named Real Oviedo manager

segments.body: Raul has been appointed manager of Real Oviedo on a contract until June 2028. The 49-year-old, who coached Real Madrid’s reserves from 2019 to 2025, replaces Julian Calero after his dismissal on Monday.

Raul won three Champions League titles and six La Liga titles with Real Madrid, scoring 323 goals in 741 appearances for the club. He also played for Schalke, Al Sadd and New York Cosmos. Oviedo were ninth in Spain’s second division when he was appointed.

content.headline: U2’s new album finds the band sounding joyful and newly sure of itself
content.shortHeadline: U2 sound renewed on Carnaval de Luz
content.standfirst: Their first album of new songs in almost nine years arrives after a turbulent stretch. A review hears a band rekindling its classic sound, while an interview traces the hard-won democracy that has kept its four members together.

image.caption: The Edge with Bono, Larry Mullen and Adam Clayton.

sources.originalTitle: U2: Carnaval de Luz review – rousing, restorative rock from a band ready to take on the world again
‘It’s a new world. It’s a little fascistic. And it needs a different response’: U2 on 50 years together – and why Bono can’t work with Trump

segments.body: With drummer Larry Mullen Jr back after medical issues, U2 sound newly energised on Carnaval de Luz, their first album of new songs in almost nine years. The review finds their familiar loud guitars, spiritual imagery and earnest uplift working again, even if not every track reaches the same heights.

segments.title: A band built to last
segments.body: In a conversation marking 50 years since the group formed, U2 describe songwriting credits shared equally and decisions made by committee as their “soviet”. The arrangement has sometimes tested the band, they say, but the Edge argues that U2 would be a different group without any one of its four members.

perspectives.body: The interview adds the band’s own account of survival: its members see shared credit and collective decision-making not as a theory but as the structure that has kept them together for five decades.

content.headline: Jorge Drexler turned a life in medicine into songs that make people dance
content.shortHeadline: Jorge Drexler finds freedom in dance
content.standfirst: The Uruguayan doctor-turned-songwriter says the effects of growing up under dictatorship took decades to leave his body. His new album returns to candombe, the music of home, as it earns eight Latin Grammy nominations.

image.caption: Musicians and participants perform in a candombe session in Montevideo.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I didn’t dance until I was 45’: how Jorge Drexler went from repressed doctor to rump-shaking Oscar-winner

segments.body: Jorge Drexler says he did not dance until he was 45. Raised in Montevideo under a dictatorship hostile to artists, he began making music while studying medicine and working as an ear, nose and throat specialist. Now 62, he has built a songwriting career that brings scientific ideas and poetry together.

segments.title: A return to candombe
segments.body: His latest album, Taracá, is a return to the candombe sound of Uruguay and follows the death of his father. It brings together Latin American musicians including guitarist Julio Cobelli and rapper Young Miko. The record is nominated for eight Latin Grammys, due to be presented on 12 November.

content.headline: Television guitarist Richard Lloyd, a force in 1970s punk, dies at 75
content.shortHeadline: Television guitarist Richard Lloyd dies at 75
content.standfirst: Lloyd’s family says he died at home in Tennessee from bile duct cancer. As a founding member of Television, he helped shape the New York punk scene around CBGB and played on the influential album Marquee Moon.

image.caption: Richard Lloyd performing in Minneapolis in 2009.

sources.originalTitle: Richard Lloyd, founding member and guitarist of punk band Television, dies aged 75

segments.body: Richard Lloyd, founding guitarist of Television, has died aged 75, his family says. He died at home in Chattanooga, Tennessee, on Saturday morning. His family said he had been diagnosed with cholangiocarcinoma, a form of bile duct cancer, in March 2026.

segments.title: A landmark guitar sound
segments.body: Television formed in 1973 and became one of the earliest punk groups to play at CBGB in New York. The band recorded two studio albums at the height of its late-1970s run; its debut, Marquee Moon, is now widely regarded as a landmark guitar record.

content.headline: At 93, Willie Nelson says he never expected to survive his hard years
content.shortHeadline: Willie Nelson on survival, loss and the road
content.standfirst: The country legend discusses his memoir, cannabis, touring and the friends he has outlived. An excerpt from the book adds his own reflections on grief, family and the habits that helped him keep making music.

image.caption: Willie Nelson.

sources.originalTitle: Willie Nelson: ‘I drank too much, I smoked too much. I took too many pills’
Stay sharp, get used to loss – and pay your taxes: the wit and wisdom of Willie Nelson

segments.body: Willie Nelson, 93, says he did not expect to live this long: “I did everything wrong.” He describes giving up alcohol after years of heavy drinking and pills, and stopping smoking cannabis at 86 after lung problems. He still uses cannabis in food and drink and says performing continues to make him feel good.

segments.title: A life turned into songs
segments.body: In an extract from his memoir, Nelson writes that grief does not disappear, but can be turned into a song. He recalls the friends who helped him through financial trouble, his family life on the road and the importance of listening. The book’s reflections complement the interview’s account of ageing and survival.

perspectives.body: The memoir excerpt offers Nelson’s own first-person perspective on loss and resilience: songwriting, he writes, has been his way of making heavy thoughts lighter, rather than pretending they can be left behind.

content.headline: Skepta’s The Fork and Knife turns grime history into a story of legacy
content.shortHeadline: Skepta looks back and moves forward on The Fork and Knife
content.standfirst: After seven years between albums, the grime pioneer moves from familiar rhythms into a portrait of a life and a wider Black British musical history. The review finds the record most compelling when Skepta makes room for the artists coming after him.

sources.originalTitle: The Fork and Knife

segments.body: Skepta’s first album in seven years takes time to find its shape, the review says, opening with some familiar grime and rap sounds. As the record unfolds, those early echoes become part of a broader look at a career spanning three decades and the many strands of Black British music.

segments.title: A wider inheritance
segments.body: The album draws together Skepta’s family history, grime, fashion, dance music and newer collaborators. On its nine-minute “Belly” cypher, the review hears the veteran MC sharing the spotlight with younger voices; elsewhere, the record presents immigrant Britain as a story of achievement and possibility.

content.headline: Kings of Leon reinvent themselves with the warm country-rock of O My Beloved
content.shortHeadline: Kings of Leon loosen up on O My Beloved
content.standfirst: The band’s tenth album turns away from the arena-rock sound that defined its biggest hits. The review hears a more spacious, country-leaning group, even as traces of its old bombast sometimes return.

sources.originalTitle: O My Beloved

segments.body: O My Beloved is a striking shift for Kings of Leon, whose recent records often leaned into a large, polished arena sound. Here the band favour warmer, more spacious country-rock, with acoustic-led songs that give the group a looser feel than it has had in years.

segments.title: Old habits remain
segments.body: The review finds the reinvention most persuasive in its quieter songs, while some bigger choruses recall the band’s late-2000s sound. The record is not without weaker moments, but its new maturity makes the group newly worth watching.

content.headline: Dream Unending’s Certain Uncertainties drifts from doom metal into cowboy jazz
content.shortHeadline: Dream Unending loosen the grip of metal
content.standfirst: The duo’s third album increasingly favours open-ended psychedelia and quieter textures over heaviness. The review admires the boldest departures, while finding the shifts less convincing when the record tries to reconcile them with doom metal.

sources.originalTitle: Certain Uncertainties

segments.body: Dream Unending continue to move away from the heaviness that shaped their earlier work. Certain Uncertainties includes long stretches with little connection to metal, drawing instead on cosmic country, spiritual jazz and open-ended psychedelia. The review calls it a striking, if sometimes uneasy, change of direction.

segments.title: Where the experiment works
segments.body: The instrumental title track and “I Carry Your Burden” are singled out for their calm, spacious sound. The review is less convinced when the record returns to heavier material, where the different styles can feel divided rather than fully fused.

content.headline: Aphex Twin’s once-divisive Drukqs now looks central to his musical legacy
content.shortHeadline: Why Aphex Twin’s Drukqs still matters
content.standfirst: A quarter-century on, the sprawling album’s collision of rave rhythms, prepared piano and digital precision feels less like a detour than a key to Richard D. James’s work. A close listen finds its tensions between dancefloor and concert hall still alive.

sources.originalTitle: Drukqs (25th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: When Drukqs appeared in 2001, its length and wild shifts in style made it difficult to place. The anniversary review hears a work that brings together the two histories of electronic music: club rhythms and the more formal experiments of the concert hall.

segments.title: The beat at the edge of rhythm
segments.body: Across the album, Richard D. James pushes percussion toward the point where rhythm becomes pitch, then sets tightly programmed piano against volatile electronic beats. The review argues that the apparent disorder is central to Drukqs: its music strains against boundaries between acoustic and electronic, human and machine, and dance music and experimental composition.

content.headline: 1 in 2 turns a filmmaker’s bowel cancer treatment into a plea to act sooner
content.shortHeadline: 1 in 2 asks why bowel cancer affects younger people
content.standfirst: David Wilkinson films his own treatment and meets people in their 20s, 30s and 40s facing the disease. His documentary asks why cases are rising among younger people and urges viewers not to delay getting tested.

image.caption: David Wilkinson in 1 in 2.

sources.originalTitle: 1 in 2 review – compassionate film about dealing with bowel cancer is a personal plea on behalf of the young

segments.body: Filmmaker David Wilkinson was being treated for stage four bowel cancer while making his previous film. In 1 in 2, he turns the camera on himself and on younger people he meets through cancer support groups, asking why a disease associated with older people is increasingly affecting people in their 20s, 30s and 40s.

segments.title: Questions without clear answers
segments.body: The film speaks with patients and NHS professionals, but finds no settled explanation for the rise. Diet and lifestyle may be factors; the possibility of microplastics is raised, not resolved. The review praises the documentary’s compassion and supports its practical message: take the bowel cancer test and do not put it off.

content.headline: A Fox Under a Pink Moon turns one teenager’s refugee journey into art
content.shortHeadline: A Fox Under a Pink Moon: a refugee’s filmed journey
content.standfirst: Soraya Akhlaghi recorded five years of flight, danger and precarious life on her phone. The resulting documentary combines that footage with animation inspired by her drawings, giving imaginative form to an experience marked by repeated uncertainty.

image.caption: Soraya Akhlaghi in A Fox Under a Pink Moon.

sources.originalTitle: A Fox Under a Pink Moon review – Iranian teen refugee paints boldly imaginative self-portrait

segments.body: Soraya Akhlaghi was 16 when she began filming her attempts to flee Iran and reach her mother in Austria. Over five years, her journey took her through asylum centres, border crossings and back to Tehran, where she lived with a violent husband. Co-director Mehrdad Oskouei assembled her phone footage remotely.

segments.title: Drawing a way through
segments.body: Akhlaghi’s drawings give the film a second language: a moon, a fox, a clown-like version of herself and figures representing her fears recur in animated sequences. The review sees this art as a source of imaginative space and resilience amid a life that repeatedly returns her to danger.

content.headline: Why Gone Girl is one writer’s dark, oddly comforting annual rewatch
content.shortHeadline: The dark comfort of Gone Girl
content.standfirst: David Fincher’s thriller is an unconventional comfort film, its writer argues: a story of marital collapse in which Rosamund Pike’s Amy turns the assumptions made about her into a weapon. The pleasure is unsettling, but that is part of the appeal.

image.caption: Ben Affleck and Rosamund Pike in Gone Girl.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Sadistic, forbidden pleasure’: why Gone Girl is my feelgood movie

segments.body: Gone Girl may seem an unlikely comfort watch: Amy Dunne disappears, her husband becomes a suspect, and the marriage at the centre of the story is full of resentment and infidelity. But this writer returns to David Fincher’s 2014 thriller each year, drawn to its carefully built tension and Amy’s revenge.

segments.title: A performance of expectation
segments.body: As the mystery turns, Amy understands how the public is likely to see a missing wife and a cheating husband—and uses those expectations to her advantage. The essay connects the film’s appeal to its sharp portrait of the “cool girl” ideal and the freedom of watching Amy refuse to be made small.

content.headline: 100 Sunset drifts through a Toronto Tibetan community in a dreamlike debut
content.shortHeadline: 100 Sunset: a quiet, elusive Toronto drama
content.standfirst: Kunsang Kyirong’s first feature follows an introverted young woman whose theft of a camcorder draws her into the lives of her neighbours. Its restrained, uncertain storytelling reflects the disorientation of its characters.

image.caption: Sonam Choekyi in 100 Sunset.

sources.originalTitle: 100 Sunset review – elliptical, elusive drama dreamlike through Toronto’s tight-knit Tibetan community

segments.body: In Kunsang Kyirong’s debut feature, 18-year-old Kunsel lives in a Toronto apartment block shared by a close-knit Tibetan community. After stealing a camcorder, she begins filming her neighbours, especially Passang, a young woman who has recently moved into the building.

segments.title: A story that refuses to settle
segments.body: Kunsel and Passang become friends, while a missing suitcase of money hints at a more conventional suspense plot. The film lets that thread recede, the review says, favouring a drifting mood that mirrors Kunsel’s inwardness and the community’s sense of displacement.

content.headline: Robert Pattinson’s reported place in the Bond race makes the casting interesting
content.shortHeadline: Could Robert Pattinson make Bond strange again?
content.standfirst: Reports say Pattinson is among the actors considered for 007. The prospect is intriguing not because his casting is confirmed—it is not—but because his appetite for odd, unpredictable roles could unsettle the franchise’s familiar shape.

image.caption: Robert Pattinson.

sources.originalTitle: Robert Pattinson has auditioned for James Bond – and finally the 007 race is interesting

segments.body: Reports from Hollywood trade publications place Robert Pattinson among the contenders for the next James Bond, alongside actors including Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, Callum Turner and Nicholas Hoult. The next 007 has not been cast, but the possibility has prompted a fresh look at what Pattinson might bring to the role.

segments.title: An unpredictable leading man
segments.body: The column argues that Pattinson’s habit of seeking out strange and varied characters could make him an unusually compelling Bond—if he were offered the part and given room to reshape it. Those are both open questions: his candidacy is reported, not confirmed, and the franchise’s handlers may prefer a more conventional approach.

content.headline: Bluey producer Daley Pearson’s film Allen turns childhood nostalgia into a story
content.shortHeadline: Daley Pearson on the childhood grief behind Allen
content.standfirst: The Ludo Studio co-founder says his new Netflix family film grew from the loss of his brother and his own attachment to childhood pop culture. Its funny story of a boy and an alien also asks what happens when nostalgia keeps an adult from moving forward.

image.caption: Allen and Daley Pearson.

sources.originalTitle: Bluey’s Daley Pearson on how losing his brother inspired his new film: ‘He was the best thing ever to me’

segments.body: Allen follows Petey, who befriends an alien as a child and struggles to move on after it leaves. Decades later, the alien returns. Director and co-writer Daley Pearson says the story draws on his own attachment to childhood memories and the fear of being held back by them.

segments.title: A loss behind the comedy
segments.body: Pearson says the story is also connected to his older brother Liam, who died of cancer when Pearson was 13. He describes the film as an attempt to understand the longing to recover something precious—and how that longing can leave a person waiting rather than living. He also wants it to work as a silly, enjoyable family adventure.

content.headline: Ava DuVernay’s 14th examines the fight over birthright citizenship
content.shortHeadline: Ava DuVernay turns to the 14th Amendment
content.standfirst: A decade after 13th, DuVernay’s new documentary explores the US constitutional amendment at the heart of a new battle over citizenship and rights. She says making the film helped her process fear and anger at what she sees happening around her.

image.caption: Ava DuVernay.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I’ve seen people in my neighbourhood pulled out of their cars’: Ava DuVernay on the cruelty and brutality of Trump’s America

segments.body: Ava DuVernay began making 14th after President Trump’s 2025 executive order challenging birthright citizenship. As she researched the amendment’s five sections, she says, she came to see attacks on more than citizenship and built the film around the wider struggle over its protections.

segments.title: A broad argument, and an open question
segments.body: The documentary brings together 50 interviews, from historians and constitutional experts to political figures and a livestreamer, to present a range of ideological and generational views. DuVernay also discusses using animation and AI to move real archival photographs, while acknowledging wider concern about the technology.

content.headline: La Bola Negra links three Spanish lives through queer history and desire
content.shortHeadline: La Bola Negra finds poetry in Spain’s queer past
content.standfirst: This three-part drama moves between 1932, 1939 and 2017 to tell stories of gay men living under different forms of pressure. The review praises its performances and visual confidence, while noting that explaining its connections can diminish some of its mystery.

image.caption: Álvaro Lafuente Calvo in La Bola Negra.

sources.originalTitle: La Bola Negra review – the complicated secrets of gay sexuality in Spain are brilliantly told

segments.body: La Bola Negra follows three men in different eras of Spanish life: Carlos, rejected by an elite club amid rumours about his sexuality; Sebastián, conscripted into Franco’s army and drawn to a Republican prisoner; and Alberto, a researcher whose inheritance unsettles his family. The film takes its title and inspiration from Federico García Lorca.

segments.title: History, memory and mystery
segments.body: The review praises the film’s performances, detailed production and the way it connects private lives to Spain’s political history. It also finds that spelling out the links between the three strands costs the story some of the mystery that makes its treatment of queer memory so affecting.

content.headline: Naturewatch brings Chris Packham’s wildlife answers to a weekly video show
content.shortHeadline: Chris Packham answers wildlife questions in Naturewatch
content.standfirst: Packham, Kyle Thomas and Megan McCubbin take on questions such as “What are wasps for?” in a new weekly video podcast, with guest experts and a promise of “guaranteed nerdiness”. The show is also due to air on BBC Two.

image.caption: Kyle Thomas, Chris Packham and Megan McCubbin present Naturewatch.

sources.originalTitle: Chris Packham’s lovely new wildlife show: best podcasts of the week

segments.body: Naturewatch is a weekly wildlife video podcast hosted by Chris Packham, Kyle Thomas and Megan McCubbin. The team answers viewers’ questions, from whether bats are really blind to what wasps contribute, with guest experts joining from a countryside base near Bristol.

The Guardian’s weekly podcast guide describes the programme as an inviting option for viewers who enjoy getting into the detail of nature. It is also scheduled to stream on Fridays at 7.30pm on BBC Two.

content.headline: The week’s TV picks include Rivals, a Zurich heist and a return to City of God
content.shortHeadline: Seven shows to stream this week
content.standfirst: This week’s guide ranges from Rivals’ mix of grief and scandal to a multi-timeline bank-heist thriller and a second season of City of God. It also points viewers towards new fantasy, true crime and a Peanuts Christmas special.

sources.originalTitle: Rivals to 12 12 12: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: Rivals returns to its world of romantic entanglements and workplace conflict after Monica’s death, while a new thriller, 12 12 12, tracks a Zurich bank robbery across a year of planning, 12 hours of action and 12 days of police work. The guide finds the latter’s plot inventive, though its characters could be more fully drawn.

segments.title: Crime and fantasy
segments.body: A second season of City of God brings a photojournalist back to the favela, where gangsters begin to consider politics as well as violence. The guide also highlights the return of The Rings of Power and two true-crime series, one focused on a murder investigation and the other on retired Hungarian detectives reflecting on police work during a transition from autocracy to democracy.
For something lighter, a new Peanuts animation gives Snoopy a Christmas-list dilemma. The guide recommends it for hitting its familiar, wholesome notes with charm and precision.

content.headline: Mums v Big Pharma follows two mothers’ campaign over sodium valproate
content.shortHeadline: Two mothers take on Big Pharma in Mums v Big Pharma
content.standfirst: This documentary revisits the harm caused to generations of children by sodium valproate and the campaign for accountability. At its centre are Janet Williams and Emma Murphy, whose persistence is set against official delay and resistance.

image.caption: Janet Williams and Emma Murphy in Mums v Big Pharma.

sources.originalTitle: TV tonight: a stirring documentary about two mothers taking on Big Pharma

segments.body: Mums v Big Pharma examines the continuing campaign over sodium valproate, an epilepsy drug prescribed despite concerns emerging during testing. The documentary follows Janet Williams and Emma Murphy, two mothers who have pushed for answers in the face of official inertia and, at times, open scorn.

content.headline: Rise of the Rockstar Chef serves up the Ramsay–Marco Pierre White feud
content.shortHeadline: Ramsay and White’s kitchen feud takes centre stage
content.standfirst: The docuseries treats the rise of British fine dining like a band story, with Gordon Ramsay and Marco Pierre White revisiting their bitter break. The review finds the rivalry gripping, if the third participant, Heston Blumenthal, is often left in the background.

image.caption: Heston Blumenthal, Gordon Ramsay and Marco Pierre White in Rise of the Rockstar Chef.

sources.originalTitle: Rise of the Rockstar Chef review – Gordon Ramsay and Marco Pierre White serve up the most sizzling TV of the year

segments.body: Rise of the Rockstar Chef revisits how Gordon Ramsay, Marco Pierre White and Heston Blumenthal helped transform Britain’s restaurant scene. The series turns chefs’ careers into a music-style origin story, complete with arguments about stolen reservations, restaurant rivalries and an eventual reunion between Ramsay and his former mentor.

segments.title: A rivalry that still simmers
segments.body: The review says the series is at its liveliest when Ramsay and White recount their conflicting versions of the feud. It also notes that the production gives White much of the spotlight and leaves Blumenthal feeling like a supporting player, while giving a revealing account of the toxic kitchen culture around the chefs’ success.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors finale finds a last-minute victory for the Faithful
content.shortHeadline: A late twist saves The Celebrity Traitors finale
content.standfirst: After a series the reviewer found flat, Sebastian’s late suspicion of Kenny changes the ending. The Faithful win £83,000 for charity, while the finale’s account of Maya’s careful deception and the players’ shifting egos gives the game a final jolt.

image.caption: The Endgame Round Table in The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: One player’s lack of ego saved Celebrity Traitors

segments.body: The Celebrity Traitors seemed headed for a win by Kenny, with most of the Faithful missing the evidence around them. After Maya is banished, Kenny chooses to end the game; Sebastian realises that a Traitor would have reason to do so, and persuades Romesh Ranganathan to change his vote. The Faithful win £83,000 for charity.

segments.title: The value of staying out of the spotlight
segments.body: The review argues that Sebastian’s lack of ego helped him notice what others missed. It contrasts his last-minute intervention with Maya’s confidence and Michael Sheen’s influential accusations, which had made him a target. After a series the writer found predictable, the reversal made the finale feel newly exciting.

content.headline: Laura Main on Call the Midwife’s pause, ageing and caring for her mother
content.shortHeadline: Laura Main on life between Call the Midwife series
content.standfirst: With Call the Midwife taking a break, Main is touring in a play about Elizabeth II and helping care for her mother in Aberdeen. She reflects on the long-running role, the value of letting Shelagh age naturally and the pressures faced by unpaid carers.

image.caption: Laura Main in By Royal Appointment.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I wanted my Call the Midwife character to age normally – even if I didn’t want to’

segments.body: Laura Main has played Shelagh on Call the Midwife since its 2012 debut, but has not filmed the show this year as it takes a sabbatical. The BBC has confirmed a sixteenth series and a film, though Main says no dates have been set. A Christmas prequel, Sisters in Arms, is planned instead.

segments.title: Work, care and ageing
segments.body: Main is touring in By Royal Appointment while helping care for her 91-year-old mother. She says the experience has made her think about the support carers need, and about the choice to let Shelagh age at the same rate as the actor playing her—even when she might personally prefer to slow the passage of time.

content.headline: A Matthew Perry documentary revisits his addiction but leaves hard questions
content.shortHeadline: The Matthew Perry documentary: moving, but intrusive
content.standfirst: Netflix’s three-part series draws on family testimony and archive footage to revisit the Friends actor’s addiction and death. The review finds it moving at times, but questions the value of asking loved ones to relive their loss without uncovering more about what happened.

sources.originalTitle: Netflix’s Matthew Perry documentary is undignified and intrusive

segments.body: The One About Matthew Perry follows the actor from his rise to fame on Friends to his work as an addiction campaigner and his death in 2023. Family members describe the generous friend they knew as well as the isolation and addiction that shaped much of his life. Much of the story, the review notes, was already told in Perry’s 2022 memoir.

segments.title: What the series leaves unexplored
segments.body: The review finds the documentary’s treatment of Perry’s death cursory, despite testimony about the ketamine he was using and the people who supplied it. It also questions the decision to linger on relatives recounting the moment they learned he had died, arguing that their distress adds little insight.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a British Asian family into the world of divorce law
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up gives its legal drama a new family
content.standfirst: The BBC spin-off moves from London to Manchester and centres a predominantly British Asian family and law firm. Its creators say it keeps the original’s mix of relationships and legal drama while making everyday British Asian lives its subject.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split Up follows Aria Kishan, a barrister expected to take over her family’s divorce-law firm, until her mother’s death changes her father’s succession plans. The six-part BBC drama moves the action to Manchester and gives the legal-family story a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team.

segments.title: Representation as ordinary life
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted to create British Asian characters living ordinary lives, rather than relying on familiar storylines about terrorism or arranged marriage. Original series creator Abi Morgan, now an executive producer, says the spin-off keeps the focus on family and relationships while supporting a new team of writers and performers.

perspectives.body: Sarma’s emphasis is not only on who appears on screen: she describes the aim as portraying a specific family truthfully, without trying to represent every facet of British Asian life through a single set of characters.

content.headline: How Grand Theft Auto grew from a crime game into a cultural colossus
content.shortHeadline: Grand Theft Auto’s life beyond the crime spree
content.standfirst: As GTA VI approaches, a feature traces the series’ changing worlds, from its early open-city experiments to the dense simulations of modern Los Santos. Its appeal, the reporting argues, lies as much in drifting through those worlds as in breaking their rules.

image.caption: Lucia and Jason, the protagonists of Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus
‘It’s so glossy and sexy!’: 10 movies (and one TV show) that inspired Grand Theft Auto

segments.body: The first Grand Theft Auto, made by Scotland’s DMA Design in 1997, offered a playful view of crime in fictional US cities. Later games built detailed open worlds shaped by film, music and literature, while moving beyond those influences into a distinct form of city-making.

segments.title: The world between missions
segments.body: The feature argues that GTA’s power is not simply its criminal fantasy. Players also remember the stretches between missions: driving aimlessly, exploring or watching the sun move across a landscape. Rockstar’s film influences—from Scarface and Miami Vice to Boyz n the Hood and Heat—helped define the series, but the games’ open worlds have become the point in themselves.

perspectives.body: A game critic interviewed for the feature describes GTA’s world as something players can inhabit rather than merely pass through: its incidental details and unhurried moments, not only its missions, create the sense of being inside a place.

segments.title: A world of contradictions
segments.body: GTA is both a satire of consumerism and a hugely profitable franchise, and a game about criminals made by a studio based in Edinburgh while depicting an American landscape. The feature suggests these tensions help explain why the series remains compelling—and why its simulated world feels so inviting in an age of artificial digital content.

content.headline: The Ocarina of Time remake makes a landmark Zelda feel new again
content.shortHeadline: Ocarina of Time becomes a modern Zelda masterpiece
content.standfirst: Nintendo’s ambitious remake keeps the original’s journeys and puzzles but adds voiced scenes, richer visuals and easier controls. The review finds that the updates deepen the story without losing its melancholy.

image.caption: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true

segments.body: The remake preserves Ocarina of Time’s familiar journey through Hyrule and its puzzle-filled temples. What changes is the presentation: expanded dialogue and fully voiced scenes bring more drama to a story that had to be told with restraint on the Nintendo 64.

segments.title: A story about time
segments.body: More flexible movement, quicker access to equipment and an orchestral score make the game easier to play and more vivid. The review also notes an alteration it dislikes—the warrior Sheik has lost some of the original’s androgyny—but finds that the remake retains the story’s central sadness: a child’s years are stolen as he is drawn into saving the world.

content.headline: A Zelda midnight launch brings fans together—and tests their patience
content.shortHeadline: The Zelda midnight launch was a long night for fans
content.standfirst: Hundreds queued on London’s Oxford Street for the Ocarina of Time remake and its limited-edition keepsakes. The writer’s four-hour wait began as a celebration of shared fandom and ended with many still waiting to be sent their collectible box.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has revived the midnight game launch – but was it worth the wait?

segments.body: About 500 fans gathered outside an Argos on Oxford Street for the midnight release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2. In an age when most games are downloaded, the launch offered a rare chance to meet fellow fans and collect a special box and ocarina-shaped keyring.

segments.title: The wait outlasts the excitement
segments.body: The writer queued for four hours before the store closed, with some customers asked to leave their details so the promised box could be posted later. The event began as a reminder of the pleasure of gaming as a shared ritual; the long wait and uncertainty about the collectables eventually wore down that feeling.

content.headline: Alex Garland’s Elden Ring film faces the challenge of making its world matter
content.shortHeadline: Can the Elden Ring film make its world matter?
content.standfirst: The game’s vast, horrific fantasy setting and a reported budget near $200m raise the stakes for its film adaptation. The central challenge, the feature argues, is not merely showing the world but giving viewers a reason to care about spending time in it.

image.caption: Elden Ring.

sources.originalTitle: Alex Garland’s Elden Ring adaptation is on course to be Hollywood’s goriest ever fantasy movie

segments.body: Alex Garland’s adaptation of Elden Ring has reportedly been shot and is in post-production, with a cast including Cailee Spaeny, Ben Whishaw and Jonathan Pryce. The game has sold more than 30 million copies, and the reported budget is close to $200m, making this a high-stakes attempt to bring its fantasy world to film.

segments.title: A world without easy answers
segments.body: The game’s horror-tinged landscapes and sparse, hostile world differ sharply from the reassurance of familiar fantasy adventures. The feature asks whether the film can turn that scale and strangeness into a compelling story, while noting that Garland’s previous films have resisted conventional happy endings. How much freedom he will have on a project of this size remains unknown.

content.headline: Replaying Call of Duty with his son turns a difficult mission into family time
content.shortHeadline: A father and son reunite through an old Call of Duty
content.standfirst: A father and his 22-year-old son revisit the co-op missions they first played when the son was five. Their renewed teamwork turns repeated failures into a moving account of how games can preserve a relationship across time.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game father and son play together.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The writer and his adult son return to the Special Ops missions in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, a game they first played together in 2009. At first their styles clash: one moves cautiously, while the other rushes ahead. They fail repeatedly, but gradually learn to work together and complete missions they never finished when the son was five.

segments.title: A bond with a deadline
segments.body: The father says the weeks of shared gaming have given him a break from adult responsibilities and a chance to feel carefree again. He and his son expect to move to different parts of the world in a few months; the son tells him he will remember this time as some of their best together.

content.headline: Stonehenge altar stone did not come from north-east Scotland, study suggests
content.shortHeadline: Stonehenge altar stone: Scotland theory ruled out
content.standfirst: New tests make a north-east Scotland origin for Stonehenge’s six-tonne altar stone very unlikely. Researchers have narrowed the search, but say its source could still lie elsewhere in Scotland, northern England or Ireland.

image.caption: Stonehenge’s altar stone lies beneath two sarsen stones in Wiltshire, England.

sources.originalTitle: Origin of Stonehenge’s altar remains enigma as north-east Scotland theory ruled out

segments.body: A new geological investigation has found it is “very unlikely” that Stonehenge’s altar stone came from north-east Scotland, challenging a theory proposed in 2024. Researchers tested samples from the stone and compared them with rock collected in the region, but have not yet identified where it originated.

segments.title: The search continues
segments.body: The study’s leader, Duncan Pirrie, said the stone definitely did not come from southern Britain, while other possible origins include elsewhere in Scotland, northern England or Ireland. The researchers say ruling out locations is part of narrowing the search; none examined so far matches the stone’s full profile.

content.headline: Tiny medical robots show promise in tests, but human use is still years away
content.shortHeadline: Medical micro-robots: promise in early tests
