content.standfirst: Researchers are developing magnetically steered devices to deliver drugs inside the body. Tests in pigs and mice are promising, but the smallest robots remain experimental and devices for use in patients are likely years away.

image.caption: Illustration of a miniature medical robot designed to deliver drugs in the gut.

sources.originalTitle: The astonishing micro-robots you swallow that spot cancer and might help treat it

segments.body: Miniature medical robots are being developed to deliver drugs to precise sites, investigate the gut and potentially treat conditions such as tumours or blood clots. One research team in Beijing reported using a 6.5mm device to deliver insulin to the lower intestine of pigs; this was an animal test, not a treatment demonstrated in people.

segments.title: From gut to bloodstream
segments.body: Other early-stage work includes a 2mm robot guided through a pig’s bloodstream and magnetic particles that heated and destroyed tumours in mice. Researchers say precise delivery could reduce the amount of a drug needed, but devices small enough to travel through human blood vessels are still some way from clinical use.

content.headline: Bird flu in Utah mink raises concern about mutation and pandemic risk
content.shortHeadline: Bird flu in mink: why researchers are concerned
content.standfirst: An outbreak on a Utah fur farm has heightened concern because mink may host both bird and human flu viruses. Experts warn that a change in the virus is possible, not inevitable, and say preparedness includes better tests and surveillance.

image.caption: Mink on fur farms may provide conditions in which a new flu strain could emerge.

sources.originalTitle: Bird flu is one mutation from serious risk to humans – how prepared is the UK?

segments.body: Bird flu has been spreading among mink on a Utah farm since at least August, according to the report. Scientists are concerned because mink are mammals with respiratory systems considered similar to humans, and could potentially host both bird and human flu strains. That creates a possibility of the viruses exchanging genetic material, but there is no report here of human-to-human spread from this outbreak.

segments.title: Preparedness questions
segments.body: The UK Health Security Agency said it has systems to detect human cases and is ready to respond. Researchers cited in the report say seasonal flu vaccination would be unlikely to protect people fully against a new pandemic strain; they also call for testing whether existing flu kits detect bird flu and for a practical exercise to develop suitable tests quickly.

content.headline: Replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives could leave some short of iodine
content.shortHeadline: Plant-based swaps may reduce iodine intake
content.standfirst: A UK dietary analysis suggests replacing dairy with unfortified plant alternatives could increase iodine deficiency, particularly among teenagers. The findings model potential dietary changes; they do not show that every plant-based drink lacks nutrients.

image.caption: People in the UK are increasingly turning to non-dairy milk.

sources.originalTitle: Tired and putting on weight? This could be the surprising reason

segments.body: A study combining UK dietary data with manufacturers’ nutrition information estimated that replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives could lower iodine intake. The modelling found that if teenagers replaced half their dairy products, 80% of girls and 72% of boys could be deficient; the researchers say teenage girls are already the group most likely to fall short.

segments.title: Fortification matters
segments.body: The risk depends on what products people choose: only one in 10 plant-based alternatives in the analysis was fortified with iodine. The Vegan Society recommends choosing fortified alternatives, and the study found that standardised iodine fortification of substitutes and bread could help avoid deficiency even if people switched entirely from dairy.

content.headline: Nvidia launches independent probe into CEO’s relationship with alleged Chinese…
content.shortHeadline: Nvidia probes CEO’s relationship amid espionage allegations
content.standfirst: Nvidia says independent directors and outside counsel will investigate reports that CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, whom US officials reportedly suspect of spying for China. The company says it has no reason to believe secrets were compromised; China rejects the allegations.

sources.originalTitle: Nvidia opens investigation after report CEO Jensen Huang was target of foreign intelligence
What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy
Nvidia will investigate CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with possible Chinese spy
What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy
Is Jensen Huang’s job on the line? Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld estimates it’s “about a 50-50”

segments.body: Nvidia’s board has opened an independent investigation after reporting linked CEO Jensen Huang to Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data-centre company Megaspeed. Jensen Huang acknowledged in a memo to staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife. US officials reportedly believe Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, but the reporting does not establish that she obtained or passed on information.

segments.title: What the probe must establish
segments.body: Nvidia’s board says it has no reason to believe that company secrets or US national security were compromised and says Huang supports the inquiry. China has called the spying allegations groundless. The BBC reports that it remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang allegedly gathered; Nvidia and Megaspeed’s roles in any transfer of information remain unresolved.

segments.title: An unusually high-stakes board decision
segments.body: Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, speaking to TechCrunch, put the odds of Huang keeping his job at “about a 50-50” and highlighted Nvidia’s central role in the AI economy and the lack of an obvious successor. That is an outside expert’s assessment, not a company decision or a finding of the investigation.

perspectives.body: Sonnenfeld’s analysis focuses on the consequences of a leadership crisis at a company that supplies chips and has financial ties across the AI industry. He also says the board will need to establish whether any technology reached China and by what route.

content.headline: US regulators reopen Waymo school-bus safety case after reports persisted
content.shortHeadline: US probes Waymo school-bus incidents after software fix
content.standfirst: The US road-safety regulator says most reported cases of Waymo robotaxis passing stopped school buses occurred after a software update intended to fix the behaviour. Its new review will assess whether the remedy was adequate.

sources.originalTitle: Waymo robotaxis kept illegally passing school buses after software fix, feds say

segments.body: The US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has opened a recall query into Waymo after reports that its robotaxis continued to pass stopped school buses with flashing lights after a software update. The regulator says a majority of the incidents it reviewed happened after the fix was deployed, and is assessing whether the remedy was adequate.

segments.title: Incidents under review
segments.body: The agency had first opened an investigation in October 2025 after video showed a Waymo vehicle manoeuvring around a stopped bus unloading children in Atlanta. School officials in Austin later reported at least five incidents. Waymo had not responded to TechCrunch’s request for comment by the article’s publication.

content.headline: UK may cut electric-car sales target, but government says no decision made
content.shortHeadline: UK EV target cut reportedly under consideration
content.standfirst: The Guardian reports ministers are expected to reduce the 2030 electric-car sales target, with a cut to about 60% among the options. The government says no decision has been taken and maintains its longer-term zero-emission commitments.

image.caption: Carmakers have warned that interim electric-vehicle sales targets are difficult to meet.

sources.originalTitle: Labour expected to cut EV targets for UK’s car industry despite MPs’ protests

segments.body: Ministers are expected to weaken the UK’s zero-emission vehicle mandate, with government sources telling the Guardian that the 2030 target could fall from 80% to about 60%, alongside an extension of compliance flexibilities. The government says no decision has been taken and says its commitment to end sales of new cars relying solely on petrol and diesel by 2030 remains in place.

segments.title: Industry and climate stakes
segments.body: Carmakers say sales are falling short of current interim targets: battery-electric vehicles made up 26.6% of new car sales in the first 10 months of the year, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders. Critics of a reduction warn it could undermine emissions plans and investment in charging infrastructure; the final policy remains unconfirmed.

content.headline: AI-generated complaints are adding to workloads across UK public services
content.shortHeadline: UK public services face a flood of AI-drafted complaints
content.standfirst: Public bodies, MPs’ offices and employers say chatbot-written complaints and requests are longer and more demanding to process. AI can help people make their case, but officials warn that inaccurate or irrelevant material is consuming scarce staff time.

image.caption: AI-generated correspondence can take little time to write but much longer for staff to process.

sources.originalTitle: ‘AI clog’: UK public bodies battle onslaught of chatbot-generated complaints

segments.body: UK public bodies and other organisations report rising volumes of correspondence drafted with generative AI, from complaints and freedom-of-information requests to legal challenges. Staff say the messages can be much longer and harder to assess than earlier submissions, even when the tools help people put their concerns into formal language.

segments.title: The cost of volume
segments.body: The Information Commissioner’s Office says AI-written requests can be repetitive, inaccurate or difficult to interpret, but still need a human response. The Guardian reports that some local-authority complaints have grown from about two pages on average to far longer; one caseworker described a 200-page submission. Public bodies are considering summaries and templates, amid concerns that filtering AI with AI could bring costs and lose the human touch.

content.headline: Meta expands Instagram’s AI system for placing suspected teens in protected…
content.shortHeadline: Meta expands Instagram’s AI teen-account system
content.standfirst: Meta says it is expanding globally a system that estimates whether Instagram users are teenagers and can place them in more restrictive Teen Account settings, even if they gave an adult birthday. The company says the safeguards include private-by-default accounts and limits on direct messages.

sources.originalTitle: Instagram’s AI age detection is expanding globally
Meta expands Instagram’s AI age-guessing tech globally

segments.body: Meta is expanding Instagram’s AI-powered age-estimation system worldwide. It looks for signals that a user may be 13 to 17 and can move the account into Teen Account protections even if the person entered an adult birth date. Meta says the settings make accounts private by default, limit some content and restrict messages from strangers.

segments.title: What the system does—and does not do
segments.body: Meta says it uses clues across profiles, including posts and biographical details, and announced the expansion amid legal scrutiny over protections for young users. The Verge’s report clarifies that this expansion concerns teen settings; identifying and removing users under 13 is a separate process. The system estimates age—it is not described as a definitive age check.

content.headline: Google plans to place ads in AI Mode follow-up answers and expand to more…
content.shortHeadline: Google brings ads into AI Mode follow-up answers
content.standfirst: Google says sponsored listings will appear in some US follow-up answers in AI Mode and is expanding AI ads to more countries. The move could give advertisers more space in conversational search while intensifying pressure on publishers seeking visits from Google.

image.caption: Google plans to expand ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode.

sources.originalTitle: Google’s AI Mode Will Soon Show Ads Even in Your Follow-Up Questions

segments.body: Google plans to show what it calls “multiturn ads” within some AI Mode follow-up answers in the US, when a conversation has commercial relevance. It is also expanding advertising in AI Mode to 10 more countries, with launches in Brazil, Mexico and the UK planned later this year, according to CNET.

segments.title: Competition for attention
segments.body: Google says sponsored product listings in AI Mode are clicked about as often as organic results. SEO specialist Lily Ray, quoted by CNET, warns that ads and AI answers could make it harder for users to find publishers’ articles through search. The extent of any further traffic decline is not established by the announcement itself.

content.headline: Medium’s TK app mixes AI writing help with private group publishing
content.shortHeadline: Medium’s TK app pairs AI writing tools with private publishing
content.standfirst: Medium’s new TK app combines note-taking, AI assistance and small-group sharing. Its launch also sharpens a debate over whether AI can support writers without taking over their work—and how readers should be told when it has been used.

image.caption: Medium’s TK writing app combines notes, AI assistance and sharing.

sources.originalTitle: Medium’s new TK app brings AI assistance directly into the writing process
Medium is launching a new note-taking app called TK

segments.body: Medium has launched TK, a writing app that can help users organise notes, get editorial feedback and fill in information while drafting. It also lets users share early work in private groups. The app is free for people with a Medium account, and Medium says authors can publish notes explaining how they used AI.

segments.title: Where assistance ends
segments.body: TechCrunch describes concerns that AI suggestions could become the writing itself, as well as limits in AI-detection tools. Medium says TK is designed to make the provenance of writing transparent; the app’s support for prompting and source material is a stated aim, not independent evidence that its tools can reliably establish how a text was produced.

content.headline: Music industry body warns Australia against weakening copyright rules for AI
content.shortHeadline: Music industry warns Australia over AI copyright proposals
content.standfirst: The head of the global recording-industry body IFPI says weakening Australian copyright protections to help AI companies train on online material would harm creators and set a damaging precedent. The government says any changes must provide meaningful control and fair compensation.

image.caption: The music industry is concerned about proposed changes to copyright rules for AI training.

sources.originalTitle: Weakening AI copyright law will spell ‘disaster for creativity’, global music body warns Albanese

segments.body: Victoria Oakley, chief executive of the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry, has urged Australia not to relax copyright rules to make it easier for AI firms to train on creative work. She argues that licensing is possible and warns that a change could affect music and culture beyond Australia if other markets follow.

segments.title: A contested policy question
segments.body: The Guardian reports that some AI companies have sought an opt-out approach, under which material could be scraped unless rights holders object. Oakley’s criticism reflects the recording industry’s position; the Australian government says it is committed to meaningful control and fair compensation. The reporting does not establish what policy the government will adopt.
